newsitem.title: UK: Bombs, bigotry shake N.Irish peace hopes.
newsitem.headline: Bombs, bigotry shake N.Irish peace hopes.

text.p: "Mindless thugs," said May Leake as she surveyed her family's charred living room, petrol-bombed in sectarian bigotry that along with guerrilla violence is hurting peace hopes in Northern Ireland.
"The living room is all burned, the sofa is all burned, there's one curtain still hanging intact and the other is lying in a heap on the floor. The carpet's burned."
Leake is a mother and a Roman Catholic and members of the Protestant community, loyal to British rule in Northern Ireland, are suspected of carrying out the fire-bombing.
But she, her sleeping husband and their four children were rescued by Protestant neighbours -- most of her neighbours are Protestants -- who were sickened by the attack.

The Leake family were victims of a bigotry that has endured for generations in Northern Ireland, a British province inhabited by Pro-British Protestants and a Roman Catholic minority that generally aspires to join with the Irish Republic.

Rising guerrilla violence and roller-coaster sectarianism have dimmed once-bright prospects for an early end to decades of conflict and the peace machine is currently mired in quicksand, all sides agree.
"It was just pure sectarianism," said Leake. "I just got the shivers, I couldn't believe what had happened."

"We have lived in this house for 16 years and we have never even had a stone thrown at the house. If it hadn't been for the neighbours banging on the door, we would have been killed..." she told Reuters in Northern Ireland's second city.

The attack was the third in two weeks on Catholics living in the mainly Protestant Waterside area of Londonderry, raising fears of a new round of the vigilante-style sectarian score-settling that has scarred the province for 27 years.
Tension is evident again with British troops in battle gear back on the streets and police at checkpoints after the breakdown of an IRA guerrilla truce nearly one year ago.

Politicians and security experts say it is a by-product of instability since the collapse of the IRA truce which, along with one by pro-British "Loyalist" groups, had given the community a peace unknown for 25 years.

The Irish Republican Army (IRA) is on the warpath again since ending a 17-month truce last February and is using its old-style tactics of hit and run and ambushing security forces to force its claim for representation at Belfast peace talks.
Britain says the IRA is goading the Loyalists to ditch their crumbling truce and re-ignite a vicious sectarian war which claimed 3,200 lives in more than a quarter of a century.

Britain says the IRA's political wing, Sinn Fein, can have a seat at the peace talks after a new truce. The IRA wants an automatic place at the talks table if it calls a new truce, and no preconditions such as the surrender of its arsenal.
On the terraced streets of Belfast's Protestant and Catholic strongholds, where gable murals glorify guerrillas and tattered flags semaphore clashing national identities, there is anxiety.
"I find people on street at the moment very, very despairing," said May Blood, a feisty white-haired battler against violence and sectarian politics, at her office on the Protestant Shankill Road.
"No one that I have spoken to in recent months...and I have spoken to (Loyalist) paramilitaries...wants the "troubles' back."
Blood, 59, a lifelong trade unionist, works with a Protestant community group trying to bring jobs and better living standards to the high-unemploymemt Shankill Road.
"Ordinary people on the street are just hoping to God that something will turn up and that we will not slide back ...
"The Loyalists have held their ceasefire and for that there is deep gratitude everywhere," she said at a building that backs on to a no-man's land road linking it a Catholic district.

"We would hope to draw in funding from a lot of different areas, from Europe, from America, from places all over the world, and if the troubles were to come back full-scale to the road we could forget about any regeneration programme we have."

Tommy Gorman, a former IRA prisoner and now a community worker in a Catholic area of Belfast where unemployment is endemic, says residents have a feeling of "frustration bordering despair". They felt the British government and pro-British parties "are implacably opposed to any sort of negotiations with republicans".
